analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal permitting for mining and processing critical minerals and rare earths from coal.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in committee and died at the end of the 117th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add projects that extract, recover, or process critical minerals, rare earth elements, and carbon from coal, coal waste, and acid mine drainage to a fast-track permitting program created by the FAST Act. Projects designated this way go through an expedited environmental review instead of the standard one. The bill would also require the Interior Department to report on how the faster permitting affects domestic supply of these materials.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal companies and mining firms that want to pull valuable minerals and rare earths out of coal seams, coal waste piles, and acid mine drainage. They would get their permits through a faster process with less environmental review, cutting time and cost.

how_it_helps.text: Adds coal-based extraction and processing of critical minerals, rare earth elements, and carbon to the FAST Act's 'critical project' definition, which subjects them to an expedited permitting and environmental review process [S2][S3].
Requires the Interior Department to report within six months on how the faster permitting affected domestic production and supply of critical minerals, rare earths, and carbon from coal [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities near mines and processing sites would face shortened environmental review of projects involving coal waste and acid mine drainage, which can carry water pollution risks. The public bears those environmental and health costs so extraction can move faster.

drawbacks.text: The bill shortens environmental review for projects that handle coal waste and acid mine drainage, materials that can contaminate water and soil if mishandled; faster permits mean less scrutiny of those risks before ground is broken [S2][S3].
Fast-tracking permits is not guaranteed to produce domestic mineral supply on its own; the bill offers no funding, purchase guarantees, or processing capacity, only a faster path to permits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill rests on a real national-security argument: the United States imports most of its critical minerals and rare earths, and coal byproducts can contain some of them. But the bill's actual mechanism is only a permitting shortcut, and it applies that shortcut to projects involving coal waste and acid mine drainage, where environmental review has real value. Supporters got a faster path to extraction; the public got reduced scrutiny of pollution risks, with no guarantee of supply in return.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee until the Congress ended, never reaching a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr (R-KY) introduced the bill on May 11, 2021 [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources and, five weeks later, to its Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill attracted zero cosponsors and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, nothing changed: coal and mining companies did not get the expedited permitting they would have gained, and communities near potential projects kept the standard environmental review. The status quo favored no one in particular, but the absence of the bill left environmental protections for coal-waste mining projects intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near mines, keeping full review

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to fast-track permitting for mineral extraction from coal, coal waste, and acid mine drainage.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Raúl Grijalva (D-AZ)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat at the subcommittee level for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican introduced the bill and no Democrat cosponsored it; with zero cosponsors of any party, it drew no recorded support or opposition votes.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal waste processors
industries.note: The bill would give these companies a faster federal permit path to mine and process minerals from coal, coal waste, and acid mine drainage. Their gain comes from reduced environmental review of projects that can pose water and soil contamination risks to nearby communities.

industries.industry: Critical minerals and rare earth producers
industries.note: Any producer extracting critical minerals or rare earths from coal-related sources would benefit from expedited permitting. A faster domestic supply of these materials is an aligned national-security goal, though the bill provides only permitting speed, not supply itself.
